title: SQL Joins: Nested Loop, Hash and Merge
summary: Quick revision notes on the three join algorithms, when the planner chooses each, how join order and indexes affect cost, and how to read join nodes in EXPLAIN ANALYZE.

chapters.title: The Three Join Algorithms
points: Join algorithm = how the engine matches rows from two inputs on a join condition; the planner picks one per join node, so one query can mix several
Nested Loop: for each outer row, probe the inner side for matches; cost ≈ outer rows × cost of one inner lookup
Hash Join: build an in-memory hash table on the smaller input (build side), then scan the larger input (probe side) and look up each row; equality conditions only
Merge Join: both inputs sorted on the join key, then walk both in step like a zipper; handles =, and sorted output is reusable by ORDER BY
Every join node has two children: the first shown is the outer (probe) side, the second is the inner (build/lookup) side

chapters.title: When the Planner Picks Each
points: Nested Loop wins when the outer side is small (few rows) and the inner side has an index on the join column: cost ≈ N index lookups
Hash Join wins for large unsorted inputs with an equality join and no useful index; cost ≈ one scan of each side plus building the hash
Merge Join wins when both inputs are already sorted (index scan or prior sort) or when sorted output is needed downstream; sort cost dominates otherwise
Non-equality joins (<, >, BETWEEN, LIKE) and CROSS joins can only use Nested Loop; Hash and Merge require = conditions
Hash Join spilling: if the hash table exceeds work_mem it splits into multiple batches written to disk (Batches > 1 in EXPLAIN), which slows it sharply

chapters.title: Join Order and Indexes That Help
points: Join order matters because intermediate result size drives cost: the planner joins the most selective pair first to shrink rows early
The planner reorders inner joins freely, but only searches all orders up to join_collapse_limit / from_collapse_limit (default 8); beyond that it follows the written order
Outer joins restrict reordering: a LEFT JOIN keeps the preserved table on the outer side, so the planner cannot swap it freely
Index the foreign key (inner side) column used in the join: it enables a Nested Loop with Index Scan and turns inner cost from a full scan into a lookup
Index on the join key also gives pre-sorted input for Merge Join; a composite index (join_col, filter_col) can allow Index Only Scan on the inner side

layout.note: foreign keys are not auto-indexed in PostgreSQL

chapters.title: Reading Joins in EXPLAIN ANALYZE
points: Run EXPLAIN (ANALYZE, BUFFERS) to get actual rows, time and loops alongside the planner's estimates; ANALYZE really executes the query, so wrap writes in a transaction and ROLLBACK
Plan reads inside-out: the deepest, most-indented child nodes run first; the join node sits above its two children
actual time and rows are per loop: multiply by loops for the true total; for a Nested Loop inner node, loops equals the outer row count
Compare estimated rows vs actual rows: a large gap (10x or more) means stale stats, so run ANALYZE; this is the top cause of a bad join choice
Hash Join shows a Hash node child with 'Buckets, Batches, Memory Usage'; Merge Join shows Sort children unless an index provides order; Nested Loop with Seq Scan on the inner side is the red flag

chapters.title: Common Join Mistakes
points: Missing index on the foreign key column makes Nested Loop do a Seq Scan on the inner table for every outer row: O(N×M)
Stale statistics after bulk loads cause underestimated rows and a Nested Loop where a Hash Join was needed; run ANALYZE after big loads
Joining on mismatched types or wrapping the column in a function (ON lower(a.x) = b.y, int vs bigint casts) stops index use; fix the types or add an expression index
Forcing plans with enable_nestloop = off in production hides the root cause; use it only to test whether another algorithm would be faster
Joining too many tables with many-to-many keys multiplies rows silently; check the join node's actual rows against the expected count

chapters.title: Join Cheat Sheet
points: Nested Loop: small outer + indexed inner, any condition; Hash Join: large inputs, equality, no index; Merge Join: pre-sorted inputs, equality
Hash spills to disk when Batches > 1: raise work_mem for that session or reduce the build side
EXPLAIN (ANALYZE, BUFFERS): read inside-out, multiply actual time by loops, compare estimated vs actual rows
Index every foreign key used in joins; run ANALYZE after bulk loads; keep join column types identical
Planner searches all join orders only up to join_collapse_limit (8); outer joins limit reordering
